title: Better tests for interstitial lung disease
official: Better tests for interstitial lung disease
summary:
Background and study aims
Doctors are currently unable to accurately predict what will happen after diagnosing their patients with one of the conditions that together represent interstitial lung diseases (ILD). This reflects the weaknesses of the tests usually employed when working towards a diagnosis. This is clearly unacceptable, and this study aims to examine potentially suitable tests for their ability to predict subsequent clinical 'behaviour' (meaning changes such as worsening symptoms, need for new treatment or admission). There is also recognised uncertainty in diagnosis with this reflecting doctors' biases towards certain conditions over others. We will work with pigeon fanciers, a group recognised to be at increased risk of lung problems, and patients with an established diagnosis of ILD, to examine several candidate tests.

Who can participate?
Active pigeon fanciers, patients recently diagnosed with ILD or patients admitted due to their ILD, aged 18 years and over

What does the study involve?
Active pigeon fanciers will undergo a blood test and a breathing test, along with supported completion of a questionnaire when attending recruitment events and annual contact from the study team to pick up any new diagnoses or tests for ILD. Patients with an established ILD will be asked to undertake blood and/or breathing tests.

What are the potential benefits and risks of participating?
Participants contribute to future clinical care through their test results being used in the assessment of candidate tests. Risks relate to blood taking (bruising, fainting) and breathing tests (if maximal effort there is potential for fainting but this is managed by sitting down during the test and this being performed by trained staff following consideration of established exclusion criteria). 

Where is the study run from?
NHS Tayside (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
January 2026 to January 2036

Who is funding the study?
1. British Pigeon Fanciers Medical Research (UK)
2. NHS Tayside (UK)

Who is the main contact?
Dr Mark Spears, mark.spears@nhs.scot
